## Where this course sits in your training {.vcenter}

::::::: roomy
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**EPIB 703 / 704: how to do it**\
Study design, bias, confounding, estimation: the tools
:::

::: msg-item
**EPIB 706: when, why, and whether**\
Which tools fit which questions, and what the field argues about
:::

::: msg-item
**Your thesis: doing it yourself**\
You'll have to defend those choices to committees, reviewers, and readers
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: notes
(~1:00) Most of you have just come through the methods sequence, which is (rightly) about learning to use the tools. This seminar is the other half: thinking about which tools fit which questions, and getting comfortable with the fact that thoughtful epidemiologists disagree about a lot. By the time you're writing a thesis proposal, nobody will tell you which estimand or design to use. You'll have to choose and defend it.
:::

## A "baker's dozen" of questions {.smaller}

:::::: {.columns .valign-center}
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**1.** What is the present and future of epidemiology?
:::
::: msg-item
**2.** What is your research question?
:::
::: msg-item
**3.** How important is formal causal inference?
:::
::: msg-item
**4.** How should we study non-manipulable exposures?
:::
::: msg-item
**5.** Should we try to randomize?
:::
::: msg-item
**6.** Do we need representative samples?
:::
::: msg-item
**7.** How should we make statistical inferences?
:::
::::::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**8.** How bad can it be?
:::
::: msg-item
**9.** To whom do epidemiologic results apply?
:::
::: msg-item
**10.** How should we communicate evidence?
:::
::: msg-item
**11.** How should we put all the evidence together?
:::
::: msg-item
**12.** Is research (including epidemiology) reliable?
:::
::: msg-item
**13.** Will AI save us or kill us?
:::
::::::
:::
::::::

::: notes
(~1:00) Don't walk through all 13. The point is the arc: we start with the discipline and the question (Units 1-2), move through design and causal inference (3-6), then inference and bias (7-9), and end with how evidence gets communicated, combined, and trusted (10-13). Every unit is framed as a question because I don't think any of them has a settled answer.
:::

## How each session works {.vcenter}

::::::: roomy
:::::: msg-list
::: msg-item
**Before class: read and annotate**\
Every reading is in Perusall; bring 2-3 points or questions
:::

::: msg-item
**Start of class: ~5 minutes of context**\
Where the topic fits in your training, and why I chose it
:::

::: msg-item
**The rest: your discussion**\
A student leads each session; I'm a participant, not a lecturer
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: notes
(~1:00) This is new this year, so flag it as an experiment and ask them to tell me if it helps. The context slides are short and are not a summary of the readings. That's the discussion leader's job. They just answer "why are we reading this, and why now?"
:::

::::::: roomy
:::::: msg-list

Sign up on the sheet (link on MyCourses)
:::

**Write one critical essay** (≤ 2500 words)\
Outline due [March 16]{.red}; final essay due [April 15]{.red}
:::

::: msg-item
**Show up, read, engage**\
The course is pass/fail and only works if we all participate
:::
::::::
:::::::

::: notes
(~1:00) Keep the admin brisk; it's all in the syllabus. Mention that the essay is a commentary in the spirit of what we read, and that at least one past essay (Goulden, Unit 3) was published. Note the AI policy briefly: I'd rather read your own thinking, and if you use these tools, say where and how.
:::
